entries.sentence: Norovirus is a very contagious stomach bug that causes vomiting and diarrhoea.
entries.note: NHS: stomach bug causing vomiting and diarrhoea; CDC: very contagious cause of vomiting and diarrhea.

entries.sentence: In the UK it often circulates in winter, though it can occur at any time of year.
entries.note: Search summary of UK health pages: common stomach bug that often circulates in winter but can occur year-round; exact page not identified.

entries.sentence: Most people recover within a few days without specific treatment.
entries.note: CDC: most people recover on their own within a few days; UKHSA: most recover in 2-3 days without medicine.

entries.sentence: Young children, older adults and people with other illnesses are at higher risk of dehydration.
entries.note: CDC: dehydration especially in young children, older adults, people with other illnesses; UKHSA adds weakened immune systems.

entries.sentence: A highly contagious viral infection of the gut that causes sudden vomiting and diarrhoea.
entries.note: NHS: symptoms start suddenly; CDC: very contagious; UKHSA: antibiotics do not work because it is a virus.

entries.sentence: Infection with norovirus, which spreads mainly by the faecal-oral route.
entries.note: Yellow Book: transmission primarily fecal-oral route.

entries.sentence: Direct contact with an infected person.
entries.note: Yellow Book: direct person-to-person contact.

entries.sentence: Eating or drinking contaminated food or water.
entries.note: Yellow Book: indirectly via contaminated food or water.

entries.sentence: Touching contaminated surfaces.
entries.note: Yellow Book: it can also spread through surfaces.

entries.sentence: Raw shellfish, especially oysters, which concentrate virus particles from contaminated water.
entries.note: Yellow Book: raw shellfish, especially oysters, frequent source because particles concentrate in filter feeders.

entries.sentence: Food handled by an infected food worker, particularly ready-to-eat cold foods such as salads and sandwiches.
entries.note: Yellow Book: sick worker example; contaminated ready-to-eat cold foods flagged as a risk.

entries.sentence: Very young or older age, or other illness, which raise the risk of dehydration.
entries.note: CDC: dehydration especially in young children, older adults, people with other illnesses.

entries.sentence: A weakened immune system, which raises the risk of dehydration.
entries.note: UKHSA: older people, young children and those with weakened immune systems at highest risk.

entries.sentence: Staying in hospitals or long-term care facilities, where outbreaks are commonly reported.
entries.note: CDC: institutional settings such as hospitals and long-term care facilities commonly report outbreaks.

entries.sentence: Close living quarters such as cruise ships, camps and dormitories.
entries.note: Yellow Book lists these as frequent outbreak settings.

entries.sentence: Eating raw shellfish.
entries.note: Yellow Book: raw shellfish frequent source.

entries.sentence: Vomiting and watery diarrhoea.
entries.note: NHS/CDC main symptoms; 'watery' from UK summary of NHS-trust pages.

entries.sentence: A high temperature in some people.
entries.note: NHS: some people get a high temperature.

entries.sentence: Signs of dehydration, such as dark urine, passing less urine than usual, or fewer wet nappies in babies.
entries.note: Search summary of NHS norovirus/dehydration pages; individual page for each item not confirmed.

entries.sentence: Dehydration, which is the main complication.
entries.note: CDC: can lead to dehydration.

entries.sentence: Severe dehydration, which may need intravenous fluids.
entries.note: CDC: severe cases may need intravenous fluids.

entries.sentence: Hospital treatment for some people, usually the very young or very old.
entries.note: Search summary of UK pages: some, usually very young or elderly, may need hospital treatment; CDC: hospital patients very old, young or ill most harmed.

entries.sentence: Diagnosis is usually based on the symptoms.
entries.note: Yellow Book: diagnosis usually based on symptoms.

entries.sentence: Laboratory testing of stool is mainly used to identify clusters of illness during outbreak investigations.
entries.note: Yellow Book: lab testing used to identify disease clusters in outbreak investigations; RT-qPCR detects virus in stool.

entries.sentence: There is no specific cure or antiviral medicine, and antibiotics do not work because the cause is a virus.
entries.note: UKHSA: no specific treatment, antibiotics don't work on viruses; Yellow Book: no antiviral agents available.

entries.sentence: Care focuses on rest and drinking plenty of fluids to prevent dehydration.
entries.note: NHS home care: fluids, rest; UKHSA: prevent dehydration by drinking plenty of fluids.

entries.sentence: Oral rehydration solutions from a pharmacy are used when there are signs of dehydration, and severe cases may need intravenous fluids.
entries.note: CDC: oral rehydration for mild cases, IV fluids for severe; UK summary: pharmacist can supply oral rehydration powder.

entries.sentence: Washing hands with soap and water is the key measure, because alcohol-based hand gels do not inactivate the virus.
entries.note: NHS and CDC: soap and water; gels do not kill norovirus.

entries.sentence: UK guidance advises staying away from work, school and hospital or care home visits, and avoiding preparing food for others, until 48 hours after symptoms stop.
entries.note: UKHSA: do not return to work/school or prepare food until 48 hours after symptoms stopped; NHS: stay away from school, work or hospitals until free of symptoms for 2 days.

entries.sentence: The CDC says no norovirus vaccine is currently available.
entries.note: Yellow Book: no vaccine or antiviral currently available.

entries.sentence: Call 999 or go to A&E for blood in vomit, green vomit in an adult, a severe headache or difficulty breathing, or for serious dehydration signs such as unusual sleepiness, dizziness on standing, or fast breathing or heart rate.
entries.note: NHS norovirus: 999/A&E for blood in vomit, green vomit in adults, severe headache, difficulty breathing; NHS dehydration: serious signs. Blended summary.

entries.sentence: NHS 111 is the route if diarrhoea lasts more than 7 days, vomiting lasts more than 2 days, fluids cannot be kept down, there is blood in the diarrhoea, or a baby or young child shows signs of dehydration.
entries.note: Search summary of NHS 111 advice.

entries.sentence: A pharmacist can advise on oral rehydration, and UKHSA asks people with symptoms to phone a GP or NHS 111 rather than attend A&E or a surgery unless advised.
entries.note: UKHSA blog: phone GP or NHS 111; pharmacist can supply oral rehydration powder.

entries.sentence: The NHS says the main symptoms of norovirus usually start suddenly.
entries.note: NHS: main symptoms usually start suddenly.

entries.sentence: They are feeling sick, vomiting and diarrhoea.
entries.note: NHS main symptoms.

entries.sentence: Some people also have a high temperature, a headache, tummy pain or body aches.
entries.note: NHS lists these.

entries.sentence: The CDC says symptoms typically begin 12 to 48 hours after exposure.
entries.note: CDC via search summary: onset typically 12 to 48 hours.

entries.sentence: Most people get better within one to three days, and the NHS says most feel better within about two days.
entries.note: CDC: 1 to 3 days; NHS: most feel better within about 2 days.

entries.sentence: UKHSA describes most people as recovering in two to three days without needing any medicine.
entries.note: UKHSA: recovery within 2-3 days without medicine.

entries.sentence: Vomiting and diarrhoea make the body lose water and salts, which is why dehydration is the main concern.
entries.note: UKHSA: vomiting and diarrhoea cause body to lose water and salts; CDC: dehydration main complication.

entries.sentence: Signs described by the NHS include dark urine and passing less urine than usual.
entries.note: Search summary of NHS advice; exact page uncertain.

entries.sentence: In babies and young children, signs include few or no tears when crying and fewer wet nappies.
entries.note: Search summary of NHS advice; exact page uncertain.

entries.sentence: The CDC says norovirus spreads mainly by the faecal-oral route, either from person to person or through contaminated food or water.
entries.note: Yellow Book transmission.

entries.sentence: It can also spread through contaminated surfaces.
entries.note: Yellow Book.

entries.sentence: The CDC says as few as 18 virus particles may be enough to cause infection.
entries.note: Search summary of CDC/Yellow Book; figure stated there.

entries.sentence: UKHSA says people are most infectious while they have symptoms but can also pass the virus on before symptoms start and after they stop.
entries.note: UKHSA blog.

entries.sentence: The CDC says people can spread it for up to 72 hours after recovering, and in some cases for two weeks or more.
entries.note: CDC summary figures.

entries.sentence: Raw shellfish, especially oysters, are a frequent source of infection, because filter-feeding shellfish concentrate virus particles from contaminated water.
entries.note: Yellow Book.

entries.sentence: Food prepared by a sick worker is another route, and contaminated ready-to-eat cold foods such as salads and sandwiches are a particular risk.
entries.note: Yellow Book.

entries.sentence: The CDC says hospitals, long-term care facilities, cruise ships, camps, dormitories and hotels are frequent places for outbreaks.
entries.note: Yellow Book lists settings; CDC background: institutional settings commonly report outbreaks.

entries.sentence: The CDC Yellow Book says diagnosis is usually based on symptoms.
entries.note: Yellow Book.

entries.sentence: Laboratory testing is used mainly to identify clusters of illness during outbreak investigations.
entries.note: Yellow Book.

entries.sentence: When testing is done, a PCR test can detect the virus in stool samples.
entries.note: Yellow Book: RT-qPCR detects virus in stool.

entries.sentence: There is no specific treatment for norovirus, and antibiotics do not work because it is caused by a virus.
entries.note: UKHSA.

entries.sentence: Care centres on resting and drinking plenty of fluids to prevent dehydration.
entries.note: NHS and UKHSA.

entries.sentence: The NHS advises against fruit juice and fizzy drinks, which can make diarrhoea worse.
entries.note: Search summary of NHS page.

entries.sentence: It also advises against aspirin for children under 16.
entries.note: Search summary of NHS page.

entries.sentence: For babies, the NHS describes continuing breast or formula feeds in small, frequent amounts, with formula made up at its usual strength.
entries.note: Search summary of NHS-linked advice; exact page uncertain.

entries.sentence: A pharmacist can supply oral rehydration powder when there are signs of dehydration.
entries.note: UKHSA blog.

entries.sentence: The CDC says oral rehydration fluids help in mild cases, while severe cases may need intravenous fluids.
entries.note: CDC.

entries.sentence: The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for blood in vomit, green vomit in an adult, a severe headache or difficulty breathing.
entries.note: NHS norovirus page via search summary.

entries.sentence: The NHS dehydration page lists unusual sleepiness, dizziness on standing, and fast breathing or heart rate as signs of serious dehydration needing urgent treatment.
entries.note: Search summary of NHS dehydration page.

entries.sentence: The NHS says to call NHS 111 if diarrhoea lasts more than 7 days or vomiting lasts more than 2 days.
entries.note: NHS.

entries.sentence: NHS 111 is also the route for a worry about a baby under 12 months, a baby or child who stops feeding, someone who cannot keep fluids down, or blood in the diarrhoea.
entries.note: Search summary of NHS 111 advice.

entries.sentence: A child under 5 with signs of dehydration, such as fewer wet nappies, is also advised to get NHS 111 advice.
entries.note: Search summary of NHS 111 advice.

entries.sentence: UKHSA asks people with symptoms not to go to A&E or a GP surgery unless a healthcare professional advises it.
entries.note: UKHSA blog.

entries.sentence: A phone call to the GP or NHS 111 is the suggested first step, and a pharmacist can advise on oral rehydration.
entries.note: UKHSA blog.

entries.sentence: Washing hands with soap and water is the main measure.
entries.note: NHS, CDC.

entries.sentence: Alcohol-based hand gels do not kill norovirus.
entries.note: NHS, CDC.

entries.sentence: The NHS says clothes and bedding soiled with vomit or faeces should be washed hot, and surfaces cleaned promptly.
entries.note: NHS and UKHSA summary; no temperature given here.

entries.sentence: UKHSA advises staying at home until 48 hours after symptoms stop, and avoiding preparing food for others for the same time.
entries.note: UKHSA blog.

entries.sentence: The NHS and UKHSA also ask people who are unwell to keep away from hospitals and care homes.
entries.note: NHS: stay away from hospitals; UKHSA: avoid visiting hospitals and care homes.

entries.sentence: In care homes and hospitals, UKHSA-linked guidance describes isolating affected residents in their own room, enhanced cleaning, and closing affected areas to new admissions.
entries.note: Search summary of UKHSA-linked outbreak guidance; exact page uncertain.

entries.sentence: The CDC says no vaccine or antiviral is currently available.
entries.note: Yellow Book.

entries.sentence: It adds that at least two vaccines were in clinical trials as of April 2025.
entries.note: Yellow Book per search summary.

entries.sentence: The CDC describes immunity to norovirus as short-lived.
entries.note: CDC via summary: immunity short-lived.

entries.sentence: It says protection against the same strain lasts between 6 months and 2 years.
entries.note: CDC via summary.

entries.sentence: The CDC also says no norovirus vaccine or antiviral is currently available.
entries.note: Yellow Book.

entries.sentence: Because no vaccine exists, hygiene measures remain the main way to reduce spread.
entries.note: Inference from sources: vaccine absent; handwashing is key (NHS, CDC).

entries.sentence: UKHSA says antibiotics do not work on norovirus because it is a virus.
entries.note: UKHSA.

entries.sentence: There is no specific treatment.
entries.note: UKHSA.

entries.sentence: Care focuses on rest and drinking plenty of fluids to replace the water and salts lost through vomiting and diarrhoea.
entries.note: UKHSA, NHS.

entries.sentence: A pharmacist can supply oral rehydration powder if there are signs of dehydration.
entries.note: UKHSA blog.

entries.sentence: UKHSA says people are most infectious when they have symptoms, but can spread the virus before symptoms start and after they stop.
entries.note: UKHSA.

entries.sentence: UK advice is to stay at home, and avoid preparing food for others, until 48 hours after symptoms have stopped.
entries.note: UKHSA/NHS.

entries.sentence: The CDC says people can shed the virus for up to 72 hours after recovery, and in some cases for two weeks or more.
entries.note: CDC summary.

entries.sentence: The NHS and the CDC both say alcohol-based hand gels do not kill norovirus.
entries.note: NHS, CDC.

entries.sentence: Handwashing with soap and water is the recommended measure, especially after using the toilet and before handling food.
entries.note: Handwashing key per NHS/CDC; 'after toilet/before food' is a textbook detail.

entries.sentence: Soiled surfaces also need cleaning, as the virus spreads through surfaces as well as by direct contact.
entries.note: Yellow Book: spreads through surfaces.

entries.sentence: The CDC says institutional settings such as hospitals and long-term care facilities commonly report norovirus outbreaks.
entries.note: CDC background.

entries.sentence: The CDC also says hospital patients who are very old, very young or very ill are most harmed.
entries.note: CDC.

entries.sentence: For this reason, UKHSA asks people who are unwell not to visit hospitals or care homes.
entries.note: UKHSA.

entries.sentence: Outbreak measures include isolating affected residents and enhanced cleaning.
entries.note: UKHSA-linked outbreak guidance via search summary.
